paras: The lynching of the "Black Kid" was the hanging of a young Black man by the Vigilance Committee of Silverton, Colorado, in late August 1881, after he was jailed in connection with the killing of the town's city marshal. Colorado papers called him the "Black Kid," while a Chicago Tribune correspondent named him Jim Catrin. Wire reports mentioned his death in a single sentence within the pursuit of the marshal's accused killers, one of whom, Burt Wilkinson, was later taken from the same jail and hanged.

According to a Silverton dispatch dated August 26, City Marshal D. C. Ogsbury had been killed "last night" by two "roughs," Burt Wilkinson and Dyson Eskridge, and the town was so aroused that "the murderers will be lynched if captured." The Tribune's correspondent at Rico traced the trouble to a shooting in a saloon on the Durango and Silverton toll road in which a saloonkeeper was killed, a row in which Wilkinson and Catrin had "figured prominently." The two then appeared on the streets of Silverton with Eskridge, and when the marshal tried to arrest them he was shot, living only long enough to name Wilkinson as his killer. The Fremont County Record reported instead that Eskridge and the "Black Kid" also fired their revolvers at Ogsbury, Sheriff Hunter and Charles Hodges.

The three men fled, and the Rico letter said nearly 100 men were on their track within minutes. Accounts differ on how the young man came into custody: a Denver dispatch said "the negro surrendered to the authorities," while the Rico correspondent wrote that he was "caught the next day." He was lodged in the Silverton jail and, according to the Rico letter, taken from it the same evening and lynched. The Denver dispatch said the Vigilance Committee of Silverton "hung him the night after Ogsbury's murder," which by the first wire's date would be about August 26. None of the reports gave the size of the party, the place of the hanging or any onlookers.

Rewards totaling $5,500 were offered for Wilkinson and Eskridge. Wilkinson was captured in the Needle Mountains by Ike Stockton, and a Denver report noted "strong feeling in favor of lynching Wilkinson." Turned over to the sheriff of San Juan County and jailed at Silverton, he was taken out by masked men between 9 and 10 o'clock on a Sunday evening in early September and hanged, while Eskridge was still at large when the Rico letter was written on September 10. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution for either hanging appears in the coverage.

Outside Colorado, the young man's death was reported mainly through a Denver dispatch of September 5, printed in the Chicago Tribune under "Arrest of Murderers" and in the Rock Island Argus, which identified him only as "a negro boy." The National Associated Press version in the Omaha Daily Bee ran as "Silverton Justice," subheaded "Summary Disposal of Three Men Interested in Oglesby's Murder," though it reported only his hanging and a rumor that the other two had been hanged. In Colorado, the Fremont County Record's state-news column first reported the "Black Kid" arrested and later listed him and Wilkinson as "murderers of Marshal Ogsbury" who were "dead. Lynched."

The Tribune's Rico correspondent called him a "coon" and wrote that "lynch law" was "most effectively dealt out to him," then gave most of the letter to Wilkinson's capture and his composure as he was hanged. That letter was reprinted in the Canton Advocate in Dakota Territory, and later briefs such as one in the Crawford Avalanche mentioned only Wilkinson's lynching.

The date of the marshal's killing varies: the first wire placed it on the night of August 25, the Fremont County Record on August 23, the New North-West on August 24 and the Mower County Transcript on the 27th. The dated Silverton wire is the most direct of these, and the Denver dispatch's "ten days ago" on September 5 agrees with it. His part in the shooting is also in doubt, since the Fremont County Record said he fired at the marshal's party, while the Rico letter and a Denver report credited the fatal shot to Wilkinson alone.

bases: A young Black man held in the Silverton jail was taken out and hanged by the town's vigilance committee (A6, A8, A11).

He was hanged by 'the Vigilance Committee of Silverton' after being jailed in connection with the marshal's killing, with no trial (A6, A8, A11); 'lynch law' and 'Lynched' are the papers' words (A10, A11).
